finding.claim: If g.user is None and a note's owner is None, can_view and can_edit both return True, so anonymous callers could read and write that note.
finding.source: g.user is None for an anonymous request, if the middleware allows it
finding.sink: can_view (notes.py:8) and can_edit (notes.py:17) return True on owner == user

trace.note: note["owner"] == user evaluates None == None as True

finding.guards_checked: No None check on the user or owner. Note creation code is not in the repo, so whether an owner-less note can exist is unverified. Low likelihood.

verdict.guard_found: none. notes.py has no None check in can_view (notes.py:8) or can_edit (notes.py:17), and the repo contains no authentication middleware that sets g.user. It is the only file in the directory.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: notes.py:8 and notes.py:17 compare note["owner"] == user with no None check, so None == None is True. The exploit needs two conditions the repo does not establish: (1) an anonymous request must reach these routes with g.user None, which depends on middleware not in the repo, and (2) a note with owner None must exist, but NOTES (notes.py:4) is never populated here and creation code is absent, so neither condition can be confirmed or ruled out.

finding.claim: The share endpoint appends any value to the shared list with no validation, dedup, size cap, or revocation path. The owner's only way to revoke access is deleting the note, which this file does not do.
finding.source: request.json["user"], supplied by the note owner
finding.sink: n["shared"].append (notes.py:45); the list is scanned linearly by 'in' in can_view (notes.py:8)

trace.note: each view scans the growing list

finding.guards_checked: Owner-only check on share (require_edit). Impact limited to the owner's own note: self-inflicted growth and no revoke or audit path. Logic gap, low severity.

verdict.guard_found: require_edit (notes.py:20-22) aborts with 403 unless can_edit (notes.py:16-17, owner == user); it is called as a raising statement at notes.py:44, so its failure does stop the append at notes.py:45.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate (notes.py:44 owner-only check, :45 unvalidated append, :8 linear scan), but the only caller that can reach the append is the note owner, who already has full control over sharing with any user via notes.py:44-45, so the missing dedup, cap, and revocation is a feature or hygiene gap rather than a security vulnerability.

finding.claim: Unknown note IDs raise KeyError, which Flask returns as 500, while existing but forbidden notes return 403. The difference reveals which note IDs exist.

trace.note: NOTES[nid] raises KeyError for an unknown ID, giving 500
require_view aborts 403 for an existing note the caller cannot view

finding.guards_checked: No existence check or uniform 404 response. Exploitability depends on whether IDs are guessable. If the app runs with debug=True, the 500 could also leak a traceback. Low severity.

verdict.guard_found: none. The only checks are require_view (notes.py:12-13) and can_edit (notes.py:16-17), which run after the NOTES[nid] lookup, so they never see unknown IDs. No existence check or uniform 404 handler exists in notes.py. The same lookup-first pattern applies to write (notes.py:34-36) and share (notes.py:43-44).
verdict.reason: The trace matches the code: NOTES[nid] at notes.py:27 raises KeyError for an unknown ID, which Flask turns into a 500, while an existing note the caller cannot view hits abort(403) at notes.py:13 via require_view (notes.py:28). Any caller that reaches these routes with g.user set (set outside this file, so the attacker's role is not visible here) can tell existing IDs from missing ones, and no effective control sits between them. The impact is low: it leaks only note-ID existence, and only if IDs are guessable.
